brief.notification_title: BTC flushed to $62K; Fed, Nvidia test the week
brief.market_summary: Markets are closed for the weekend, so the stock, bond and oil numbers below are Friday's closes. Only crypto has traded since the last brief. The S&P 500 finished the week up about 2.5% at 7,561.67, but money kept rotating out of tech: XLK is -10% and SMH -12.9% over a month, while staples, health care and financials are each up about 6%. Treasuries sold off hard. The 10Y rose 29.5bp on the week to 5.154% and the 5Y 33bp to 4.98%, as markets moved to near-certainty on a December Fed hike. Brent has fallen two weeks running to $95.84 as OPEC+ supply comes back. Over the weekend crypto flushed out leveraged longs: BTC hit about $62K, its lowest since mid-July, on roughly $1.96B of liquidations, and has since bounced to $64,717.
brief.since_last: Stocks, Treasuries and Brent haven't traded since the last brief, so those levels are unchanged. Crypto took the next leg down. About $1.96B of positions were liquidated in 24 hours, mostly longs ($645M in BTC, $432M in ETH). BTC traded near $62,000, ETH near $1,711 and SOL near $67.60 before bouncing (n80, n89, n54). Spot BTC ETFs have now had seven straight days of outflows, about -$2.1B so far in November (n11). Weekend coverage is more hawkish: Fed officials are said to be signalling a December hike and possibly another in January (n56). Analysts are calling for Brent to test $90-92 this week (n53, n71). One report says OPEC+ meets today (Sunday) and will keep output targets unchanged (n116). That conflicts with research putting the next full ministerial on 29 Nov, so treat it as unconfirmed. Analyst sentiment on Nvidia after Huang's exit has turned more negative (n27), and Megaspeed has opened an internal probe into reports linking Jensen Huang to a former executive (n120). On the previous ETH trim: ETH was around $1,915 about an hour after the 00:00 UTC Saturday close (back-calculated from $1,724 at -10% in 24h). The $2,000 backstop very likely triggered, but confirm on your own venue.

economic_data.takeaway: Slightly softer than consensus, but the 10Y still rose 5bp on Friday to 5.15%. Rates are being driven by the Fed's hiking signals and weak 10Y/30Y auctions (n144), not by this print. A 6.5% y/y pipeline inflation rate keeps a December hike on the table.
In line, and well below September's 0.8%. But core y/y is stuck at 5.0%, so it gives the Fed no reason to back off.

economic_data.takeaway: Retail sales are expected at +0.8% (prior 1.1%) and year-to-date fixed-asset investment at about -6.9%. A weak set would add to the oil demand worries on top of OPEC+ supply. Copper is already at about a four-month low (n154).
A big drop is already expected. Only a miss well below 10 would ease hike pricing much.

This is the key US print of the week. A hot number on top of 6.5% PPI makes December close to a lock and pushes the 2Y and 5Y higher. A miss is the main thing that could pull bill yields back toward 4%. Note the consensus varies by source (0% to +0.3%).
Sources disagree on the prior (0.9% vs 0.1% for the control group), so judge the release by the surprise against consensus, not the change from last month.
A hot print would strengthen the BOE's case to hike (n126) and add to the global rise in yields.

Cook and Hammack dissented in favour of a hike in October. Watch how many other members leaned the same way and whether anyone discussed a larger move (n167). Hawkish minutes would come out the day after Nvidia reports.
Claims near 200K describe a tight labour market. Revisions already show the job market is stronger than first thought (n133). Nothing here argues for a pause.
Expectations above 4% are exactly what a hiking Fed is worried about. An upward revision would back up the hawkish speakers.

earnings.result: Consensus EPS $2.49 (vs $1.24 a year ago), revenue about $108.8-109.5B. Options imply about ±9% by the end of the week. Interim CEO Colette Kress hosts the call.
earnings.takeaway: The stock fell about 13% last week after Jensen Huang resigned. Beating the numbers won't be enough on its own; what matters is whether guidance from new leadership is believed. It is the biggest single swing factor for SMH, the Nasdaq and AI-linked names like AMD, Broadcom and CoreWeave, and copper has been trading off the same story (n154).

earnings.result: Strong results and a positive outlook according to coverage. I don't have the actual EPS vs estimate. The stock rose after hours, then fell about 6% on Friday.
earnings.takeaway: A good report sold hard tells you positioning in AI infrastructure is crowded. Expect the same 'sell the news' reflex around Nvidia.

earnings.result: Beat expectations (exact EPS and revenue not retrieved). The stock fell about 3%.
earnings.takeaway: Another beat that was sold. It adds to the case for staying out of SMH until Nvidia has reported.

earnings.takeaway: A test of housing-linked spending with mortgage rates at 7.11% (n153) and the 10Y at 5.15%. It reports the same morning as retail sales. Lowe's follows Wed ($2.86 vs $3.06 a year ago).

earnings.takeaway: A defensive bellwether. Staples (XLP) are already +6.5% over a month, so the bar for a beat is higher. Target ($2.03, Wed) and TJX ($1.33, Wed) round out the read on consumers.

earnings.result: Consensus EPS $0.52 vs $0.53 a year ago.
earnings.takeaway: A large software name reporting the night after Nvidia. It will show whether the selling in tech spreads beyond hardware.

sections.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their first weekly gain in five weeks, but Friday showed the same split as the month. Tech fell (XLK -2.0%, SMH -3.0%, AMD -9%) while staples, energy and financials rose. This week's results hinge on Nvidia (Tue) and the Anthropic IPO, both arriving with the 10Y above 5%.
key_points: S&P 7,561.67 (+2.5% on the week, -2.4% over a month). Nasdaq 25,136 (-5.9% over a month). The Dow is +0.3% over a month. NQ futures closed -1.23% on Friday.
Leaders over the month: XLV +6.6%, XLP +6.5%, XLF +6.2%, XLY +5.8%. Laggards: XLK -10.0%, SMH -12.9%.
NVDA lost about 13% on the week after Huang's exit. Cisco (-6%) and AMAT (-3%) fell despite beating. The VIX is 19.3, down 25% on the week, so hedging is cheaper going into Nvidia.
The Anthropic IPO this week could pull money out of existing AI names. MarketWatch notes the SpaceX IPO coincided with June's semis peak (n14).

sections.summary: Treasuries had a bad week. The 5Y rose 33bp and the 10Y 29.5bp to 5.15%. The trigger was hot inflation, weak 10Y and 30Y auctions, and Fed officials openly supporting hikes in December and possibly January. The belly of the curve (5Y) sold off most, which means markets are pricing Fed policy, not just a term premium.
key_points: Weekly moves: TLT -3.1%, IEF -2.0%, LQD -1.65%, SHY -0.56%. HYG is only -0.38%, so this is a duration selloff, not credit stress.
The Fed funds rate is 3.75-4.00%. Markets see a December hike as near-certain (n157), and Collins prefers gradual hikes (n158).
Mortgage rates fell to 7.11% (n153), but that survey predates the latest jump in yields. Expect them to rise again.

sections.summary: Brent settled at $95.84 for a second weekly loss of 2.5%. It is about 20% below the late-October high near $118 and touched $91.49 on Tuesday. Supply returning is outweighing the headlines: OPEC+ output jumped 2.04M bpd in October, and unconfirmed Houthi attack claims gave only a one-day lift.
key_points: OPEC+ crude output is 41.23M bpd, within 3% of the pre-war baseline. Saudi output rose to 10.56M bpd from about 8.37M.
Analysts see Brent testing $90-92 this week (n53, n71). The bear level to watch is $91 and the bull level $98 (n128).
One report says OPEC+ meets Sunday and will hold targets (n116). Research points to 29 Nov instead, so this is unconfirmed.

Upside risks: Iran–US talks on Hormuz, tanker incidents, and strategic reserve buying through 2028 (n32). EIA inventories are out Wed 10:30 ET. XLE rose 5.4% on the week even as Brent fell, which is a divergence worth noting.

sections.summary: Crypto had its fourth capitulation-style flush since the BTC record. Short-term holders who bought above $80K sold, and about $1.96B of positions were liquidated. BTC broke its 200-day moving average near $73K, hit about $62K and has bounced to $64,717. Behind it: rising rates, a stronger dollar and seven straight days of ETF outflows.
key_points: BTC $64,717 (-13.8% on the week, -20.2% over a month). ETH $1,804 (-18.1% / -25.5%). SOL $71.34 (-18.8% on the week, low $67.60). XRP $0.957, a two-year low below $1 (n109).
Spot BTC ETFs: -$185M Friday, -$1.07B on the week, about -$2.1B in November (n11). ETH ETFs: +$2.4M Friday, ending a six-day outflow run, but -$399M on the week.
Glassnode maps a liquidation cluster at $60-62K (n19). Losing $62K on a daily close would open that zone.

Some buyers are stepping in. Wallets linked to Erik Voorhees bought about 48.6K ETH for $97M (n76), and Strategy and Strive hint at more BTC buys (n8). That isn't enough to offset the ETF selling. TON has held up best (-1.25% on the week).

brief.instructor_take: My read is that rates are what matter this week. Nvidia will get the headlines, but the bond market is driving everything else. The 10Y rose 30bp in a week to 5.15% and the 5Y rose 33bp. Look at what moved with it: gold fell 4.6%, BTC fell 13.8% and the dollar index rose 1.1%. When cash pays 4.3% and the Fed is hiking, assets that pay no yield get repriced first. That is what crypto and gold went through this week. Here's what a less experienced investor would miss: Friday's PPI actually came in a touch below consensus, and yields still rose. So it isn't one inflation print that's pushing rates. It's auction supply and Fed officials talking up hikes, and those don't reverse on one soft number. Stocks rose 2.5% anyway, but look at what led: staples, health care and financials. That's money hiding out and banks benefiting from higher rates, not risk appetite. The week is packed: Warsh on Monday, retail sales and Nvidia on Tuesday, FOMC minutes on Wednesday, plus the Anthropic IPO. Each one could cause a gap move, and with no options or leverage you can't hedge a gap, so the edge is in sizing and waiting. I would keep dry powder in T-bills, stay out of semis until Nvidia's guidance has been tested, and finish the pre-committed ETH trim without chasing more selling. What would change my mind is a soft retail sales print plus dovish-leaning minutes that pull the 2Y below about 4.75%. That would be my cue to start thinking about duration and risk again.

top_ideas.title: Park dry powder in T-bills while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.one_liner: Bills pay ~4.1-4.3% and gain from each hike; let the week play out
top_ideas.thesis: With a December hike close to priced and January in play, 0-3 month bills reset higher within weeks of each hike while longer bonds lose money. SGOV earns roughly 4.1-4.3% while Nvidia, the Fed minutes and the Anthropic IPO play out, and it is the funding pot for the SMH re-entry rule.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start from the policy path. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% with two dissents in favour of a hike, and officials are now signalling December and possibly January (n56, n157). The 3-month par yield is 4.32% and the 6-month 4.42%. Bills mature every few weeks, so SGOV rolls into each new, higher rate almost straight away. That's why it holds its value while TLT fell 3.1% and LQD 1.65% last week. I'm choosing SGOV over SHY because SHY carries about two years of duration, and the 2Y at 4.88% still has room to rise in a hiking cycle; SHY lost 0.56% last week. The concept here is opportunity cost: with 4%+ available risk-free, any equity or crypto trade has to earn more than that to justify itself. Most investors treat cash as doing nothing, but at these yields holding it is a deliberate position. What would prove me wrong is the 13-week bill yield falling below 4.0%, because that would mean the market has started pricing cuts and it's time to lock in longer duration.

top_ideas.entry: Buy at market after Monday's open with idle cash. Add the ETH/ETHA trim proceeds once they settle. No price level is needed.
top_ideas.invalidation: Exit if the 13-week bill yield falls below 4.0%, which would mean the market is pricing cuts. Otherwise, redeploy part of it only when the SMH re-entry rule triggers.
top_ideas.sizing: All idle cash plus the trim proceeds, comfortably 15-30% of the portfolio, since it works as a cash equivalent

top_ideas.title: Stay out of semis through Nvidia and Anthropic
top_ideas.one_liner: No semis buys until NVDA guides well and SMH holds $500 two days
top_ideas.thesis: SMH (486.75) is down 12.9% over a month. Its biggest holding reports Tuesday with an interim CEO, an implied move of about ±9%, and a market that just sold beats from Cisco and AMAT. Waiting costs little; being wrong before the print costs a lot.
top_ideas.reasoning: Start with the price action: Cisco fell 6% and AMAT 3% after beating, which tells me positioning in AI hardware is still crowded and good news is being used as a chance to sell. Then add the governance discount. Nvidia lost 13% on the week after Huang resigned, and the Megaspeed probe keeps that story alive (n120). So Tuesday's result will turn on whether Colette Kress's guidance is believed, not just on whether EPS clears $2.49. On top of that, a 5.15% 10Y compresses valuations on long-duration growth stocks, and the Anthropic IPO competes for the same AI money (n14). I'd use SMH rather than NVDA itself for the eventual re-entry, because it spreads the single-name governance risk across the chip sector. The concept is event risk with asymmetric information: after the print you give up maybe 5-10% of upside, but you remove a ±9% gap you can't hedge. What would change my mind is a beat and raise followed by SMH closing above $500 on both Wednesday and Thursday. That would show buyers absorbing supply rather than selling the news.

top_ideas.entry: No buying through Thu 19 Nov. If NVDA beats and guides above consensus, buy half the trimmed amount once SMH has closed above $500 on Wed 18 and Thu 19. Buy the second half after Anthropic has traded two sessions with SMH still above $500. Fund both from SGOV.
top_ideas.invalidation: The avoid ends if NVDA beats and raises and SMH closes above $500 on two straight sessions after the report. If that happens, rebuild in the two halves above.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new exposure now. On re-entry, half of the previously trimmed semis allocation per step (e.g. 1.5-2% of the portfolio each)

top_ideas.title: Finish the ETH backstop trim, then stop selling
top_ideas.one_liner: ETH backstop below $2K likely fired: finish the trim, keep the core
top_ideas.thesis: ETH was around $1,915 shortly after the 00:00 UTC Saturday close and is $1,804 now, so the $2,000 backstop almost certainly triggered. Finish the remaining third as planned, put the proceeds into SGOV, and then leave the core alone. The flush makes further selling poor value.
top_ideas.reasoning: I set this rule ahead of time so we wouldn't have to decide in the middle of a crash, and that's what this weekend is. The evidence is still negative. ETH is -18% on the week against BTC's -13.8%, so it is acting as the high-beta version of the same rate and dollar squeeze. ETH ETFs lost $399M on the week, and one +$2.4M day doesn't reverse that. A 5% bounce from the $1,711 low is noise. I'm trimming ETH rather than BTC because ETH has the weaker flows and the bigger drawdown (-25.5% over a month). I'm also candid that the $432M of ETH long liquidations and the roughly $97M Voorhees-linked buy (n76) look like a washout, and that's why this is only a third of the position and stops there. Many investors read 'capitulation' as a reason to skip a risk rule. I read it as a reason not to sell the core, which is a different thing. What would bring me back in is a full week of daily closes above $2,000 plus three straight days of ETH ETF inflows.

top_ideas.entry: Confirm your venue's 00:00 UTC Saturday daily close. Evidence says it was about $1,900, below $2,000. If the trim isn't done yet, cancel any unfilled $2,150/$2,200 limits and sell the remaining third today in two spot orders a few hours apart. For ETHA, sell at Monday's open. Proceeds go to SGOV.
top_ideas.invalidation: If your venue shows the Saturday close at or above $2,000, the backstop didn't fire, so don't sell. After the trim, no further selling of the core. Consider rebuying only after a week of daily closes above $2,000 plus three straight days of ETH ETF inflows.
top_ideas.sizing: Only the remaining third of the planned trim. The core ETH position stays untouched.

brief.prior_ideas_review: 1) BUY SGOV: no US trading since the last brief. The thesis is stronger, not weaker: the weekend headlines firm up the December hike (n56, n157), and the 13-week bill is 4.12% with the 3M par yield at 4.32%. Keep it. 2) AVOID SMH: SMH still sits at Friday's 486.75, below the $500 re-entry level. Nvidia's tone has worsened (n27, n120). Keep the rule as written. 3) TRIM ETH: very likely triggered. ETH was around $1,915 an hour after the 00:00 UTC Saturday close, fell as low as about $1,711, and is $1,804 now. If you sold over the weekend, fills were probably somewhere in $1,720-1,900. That was painful but it worked as designed, cutting exposure ahead of a further 5-10% drop. If it isn't finished, complete it today (spot) or at Monday's open (ETHA), then stop. lesson.concept: Opportunity cost: why rising real yields hit assets that pay no yield
lesson.explanation: An asset that pays no income, like gold or bitcoin, competes with whatever cash earns risk-free. When T-bills yield 4.3% and the Fed signals more hikes, holding a zero-yield asset costs more each month. When the dollar strengthens as well, global buyers pay even more for it. The assets that rose most on cheap money and speculative leverage tend to be repriced first and hardest.
lesson.todays_example: Over the week the 10Y rose 29.5bp to 5.15% and the dollar index 1.1%. Meanwhile gold fell 4.6% (n43), BTC 13.8% and ETH 18.1%, even though the S&P rose 2.5%. The same force explains why SGOV, which gains from each hike, is idea #1.
